spec.full_target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
spec.conclusion: For every r>0 the function x↦e(x,r) is Lebesgue integrable on V; E is differentiable on (0,∞), and E'(r)=0 for every r>0. In particular E(s)=E(t) for all s,t>0. The energy is ∫_V (|u_t|^2+sum_{j=1}^n|u_j|^2) dx, with no factor 1/2 and no assertion at time zero.

definitions.type: real Euclidean vector space with measure
definitions.definition: V=R^n, realized as tuples (x_1,...,x_n). Its topology is the Euclidean topology and its measure dx is the product of n one-dimensional Lebesgue measures. Compactness, continuity and derivatives use these topologies; integrable means Lebesgue absolutely integrable.

W=R^m with inner product v·w=sum_{k=1}^m v_k w_k and norm |v|=(sum_{k=1}^m v_k^2)^(1/2). On V the same convention uses n coordinates. The squared norm and dot product in all formulas have this meaning.

u_t(x,r) is the derivative at r of the one-variable map ρ↦u(x,ρ). Derivatives are ordinary Fréchet derivatives in coordinate directions; outside their differentiability set use the total derivative convention zero. This convention grants no differentiability.

definitions.type: family indexed by j=1,...,n of functions V×(0,∞)→W
definitions.definition: u_j(x,r)=∂_{x_j}u(x,r), the coordinate derivative in the jth spatial direction.

definitions.definition: u_jt(x,r)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,r). Commutation with ∂_r u_j is a claim to be proved, not part of this definition.
Δu(x,r)=sum_{j=1}^n u_jj(x,r), component by component. The gradient D_x u has columns u_j; its Frobenius square is sum_{j=1}^n |u_j|^2.
e_t(x,r)=∂_r e(x,r), with the total derivative convention of D003.

propositions.statement: Let X be a measurable space, μ a measure on X, Z a normed additive commutative group and normed real vector space, I an index type and l a countably generated filter on I. Let Φ:I→X→Z, φ:X→Z and β:X→R. Suppose eventually along l the functions Φ(i,·) are almost everywhere strongly measurable; eventually along l, |Φ(i,z)|≤β(z) for μ-almost every z; β is μ-integrable; and for μ-almost every z, Φ(i,z) tends along l to φ(z). Then ∫_X Φ(i,z) dμ tends along l to ∫_X φ(z) dμ.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and put J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Its endpoints satisfy 0<t0/2<3t0/2, so H006 supplies a compact spatial set C on whose complement u=q for every time in J. Compact sets in Euclidean space are closed; hence (V\C)×int J is open. At each of its points u agrees with the constant q on a neighborhood. Every positive-order derivative is therefore zero there: difference quotients of a locally constant function are zero, and this applies successively to all orders. H002 gives continuity of all derivatives on the entire open domain.
Apply M009 to the compact set C and the identity map V→V. The identity is continuous, so it gives a real uniform norm bound even when C is empty.

argument.text: Define Xhat to be the tuple space of all coordinates except j with product Lebesgue measure, and χ(x)=((x_i)_{i≠j},x_j). Apply M011 with predicate i≠j to split the finite product measure. The remaining block {j} has a unique element; M017 identifies its product measure with ordinary one-dimensional Lebesgue measure by evaluation at j. Composing these explicit measurable equivalences shows that χ is a measure-preserving measurable equivalence from V to Xhat×R. The inverse is coordinate insertion. When n=1, Xhat is the one-point empty product with mass one, so the same identification applies.

argument.text: Fix any y∈Xhat and define G(z)=g_j(χ^{-1}(y,z),t0). By N003 this function is smooth and G'(z)=∂_{x_j}g_j(χ^{-1}(y,z),t0). If z=±R, the inserted point lies outside C, since C⊂(−R,R)^n; hence G(−R)=G(R)=0. The derivative is continuous on the finite interval [−R,R], so it is interval integrable there. M006 gives ∫_{−R}^R G'(z)dz=G(R)−G(−R)=0. This is also the integral on the closed interval: its endpoints have Lebesgue measure zero. For |z|>R the derivative vanishes by F001; thus ∫_R ∂_{x_j}g_j(χ^{-1}(y,z),t0) dz=0. This proves the zero inner integral for every y, including when some other coordinate lies outside the box.

It is continuous and supported in the compact product box corresponding to Q, hence integrable; equivalently integrability follows by transport through the measure-preserving measurable equivalence in F002 from F001. Apply M016 with the coordinate equivalence χ and scalar function H: ∫_V ∂_{x_j}g_j(x,t0)dx=∫_{Xhat×R}H. Apply M007 to this integrable H. The product Lebesgue factors are sigma-finite, hence s-finite, including the empty factor. F003 makes each inner integral zero. Therefore ∫_V ∂_{x_j}g_j(x,t0)dx=∫_{Xhat}0=0. Restricting to Q gives the identical box integral, since its integrand vanishes off Q. This is precisely the coordinate FTC/Fubini integration-by-parts step.

Integrate the identity in F001 and use M013 with its two integrable summands B_j(·,t0),T_j(·,t0). F004 yields 0=∫_V B_j+∫_V T_j. Rearranging gives ∫_V B_j=−∫_V T_j. Unfold the definitions of B and T to get exactly the asserted vector-dot-product formula. Generalize over t0>0 and all spatial indices j.

argument.text: Fix t0>0. N002 supplies integrability of e and every derivative product at this time. N004 gives E'(t0)=∫_V e_t(x,t0)dx. N003 gives e_t=2A+2sum_{j=1}^n B_j pointwise.

produces.statement: E'(t0)=∫_V e_t(x,t0)dx, e_t(·,t0)=2A(·,t0)+2sum_{j=1}^n B_j(·,t0), and all these scalar sections and each T_j(·,t0) are integrable.

argument.text: Use M013 for the two terms in e_t, M014 to take the factors 2 outside the integrals, and M012 for the finite sum of integrable B_j sections. Then use N005 for every j. This retains the exact calculation E'(t0)=2∫_V u_t·u_tt dx+2sum_j∫_V u_j·u_jt dx=2∫_V u_t·u_tt dx−2sum_j∫_V u_t·u_jj dx. Every integral is finite by F001.

produces.statement: E'(t0)=2∫_V A(x,t0)dx−2sum_{j=1}^n∫_V T_j(x,t0)dx.

argument.text: Apply M012 also to the finite family T_j and use M013 and M014 with scalar −1 to combine the difference of integrals. By finite distributivity of the dot product and Δu=sum_j u_jj, A−sum_j T_j=u_t·(u_tt−Δu) pointwise. Thus F002 becomes E'(t0)=2∫_V u_t(x,t0)·(u_tt(x,t0)−Δu(x,t0))dx. N001 makes this integrand zero at every x, so its integral and E'(t0) are zero.

The time t0 was arbitrary. N002 gives integrability for every positive time, N004 gives differentiability on (0,∞), and F003 gives the zero derivative there. The definitions e=|u_t|^2+sum_j|u_j|^2 and E=∫e preserve the required energy normalization without a factor 1/2.

produces.statement: For every ρ>0, e(·,ρ) is integrable, E is differentiable at ρ and E'(ρ)=0.

argument.text: For completeness fix arbitrary s,t>0. If s<t, restrict E to [s,t]; F004 gives differentiability there and within derivative equal to its ordinary derivative zero. M005 with bound 0 gives |E(t)−E(s)|≤0(t−s)=0, hence E(t)=E(s). If t<s, apply the same argument on [t,s], and if s=t equality is immediate. The source expects a total real function: extend E arbitrarily outside (0,∞); it agrees with E on an open neighborhood of either closed interval, so its derivatives there are unchanged. Generalizing over s,t gives constancy. Together with F004 this proves every clause of P. All arguments concern positive times only.
